title: Detection Strategy for Financial Theft
summary: This strategy detects financial theft, where an adversary uses a valid account or a compromised business process to move money or redirect a payment. Typical activity includes creating a new payee, editing bank account details on a supplier record, approving a large first payment and hiding the confirmation replies with a mailbox rule. Visibility comes from payment platform audit records, enterprise resource planning change logs, mailbox configuration audit entries and endpoint process activity on finance workstations. It fails in practice because finance staff create payees and release payments every day, so the detection lives or dies on peer baselines and on catching the rare combination of a brand new payee and an immediate large payment.

beginner.definition: Financial theft means an attacker steals money, not just data. This detection watches payment systems and finance computers for the steps of that theft. It looks for new payees, changed bank details and unusual payments. The goal is to catch the fraud before the money leaves the company.
beginner.whyItMatters: Money lost to fraud is often gone for good, because bank transfers complete in minutes. One changed bank account number on a supplier invoice can cost more than a full data breach. An attacker needs only one mailbox rule and one approved payment to succeed. Logs alone cannot stop this, so the detection pairs records with a fast human check.
howItWorks: Payment and enterprise resource planning systems write an audit record for each important action.
These records include the user, the payee, the amount and the time of the change.
The rule builds a normal pattern for each finance user over several weeks.
A new payee followed quickly by a large payment breaks that pattern and is scored.
Mailbox rules that hide bank messages are added as supporting evidence.
The alert goes to the fraud team with the account number and the approving user.
beginner.example: Picture a shop till that prints a receipt for every sale. A dishonest cashier cannot simply take notes from the drawer, because the till records each one. Instead he adds a fake supplier to the payment list and pays that supplier for goods that never arrive. The receipt looks completely normal, but the supplier list changed. This detection watches the supplier list, not the drawer.
takeaways: Watch the change to the payee record, because the payment itself often looks normal.
Correlate mailbox, endpoint and payment logs to see the whole story.
Set a fast human check for any new payee with a large first payment.

objectives: Describe the common steps in a business email compromise payment fraud.
Name the audit records a payment platform produces for each action.
Build a baseline of normal payee creation for finance staff.
Correlate mailbox rule changes with payment events on the same account.
Design an escalation path that reaches the fraud team within minutes.
dataSources: Payment platform audit records for payee creation, bank detail change and payment approval
Enterprise resource planning change logs for vendor master records and purchase orders
Cloud mailbox audit entries recording inbox rule creation and automatic forwarding settings
Windows Security event 4688 process creation on finance workstations with command line auditing
Bank portal audit records showing login source address, downloaded statements and new beneficiary setup
logic: The pattern links a change in payment data with a payment that follows it very quickly. Analysts must correlate the user account, the payee identifier, the bank account details and the timestamps from payment platform audit records, then add supporting evidence from mailbox rules or endpoint process creation on that same account. Normal finance work shows a payee created days or weeks before its first payment, with review by a second person, and edits made during office hours from a known workstation. The malicious case shows a first payment to a brand new payee, often close to the payment run deadline, with the bank account recently edited and a hidden inbox rule that suppresses replies from the real supplier.
pseudoQuery:
# title: New Payee With Immediate Large Payment
# logsource:
#   product: windows
#   service: payment_platform
# detection:
#   selection_new_payee:
#     action:
#       - 'payee_created'
#       - 'bank_details_changed'
#   selection_large_payment:
#     action: 'payment_approved'
#     amount: '>10000'
#   timeframe: 24h
#   condition: selection_new_payee and selection_large_payment
# level: high
falsePositives: Quarter end payment runs that register several new suppliers and pay them in the same week
A legitimate supplier change of bank details confirmed by telephone and processed by two reviewers
Treasury operations moving funds between the company's own accounts under a standing instruction
tuningNotes: Baseline payee creation and payment size per finance team for one quarter, then set the amount threshold above the ninety-fifth percentile of normal first payments. Scope the rule to accounts that hold payment release rights, and exclude the automated accounts payable batch account that creates payees by design. Add a filter for changes that carry two distinct approver identifiers, because dual control is the strongest benign signal you have. This reduces noise from routine supplier onboarding, but you lose visibility of fraud carried out by two colluding insiders who both approve the payment.
